column2: [Marutta] "I see a marvel today: Fire has come in bodily form. Bring a seat, water, foot-water and a cow, sage."
[Agni] "I accept your seat, water and foot-water, blameless one. But know that I have come as a messenger sent by Indra."
[Marutta] "Is the glorious king of the gods well, and happy? Is he pleased with us, smoke-bannered one? Are the gods rightly under his control? Tell me all that, god."
[Agni] "Shakra is very happy, lord of kings, and wishes an unfading friendship with you; all the gods are under his sway, O king. Hear the message of the king of the gods.
The reason he sent me to you is to give Brihaspati to Marutta: this teacher, king, will officiate for you and make you, though mortal, immortal."
[Marutta] "Samvarta, the brahmin, is my officiant; this is Brihaspati's request, and that one, having officiated for the god Mahendra, would not look well officiating for a mortal today."
[Agni] "If Brihaspati officiates for you, by the favour of the king of the gods you will gain the great worlds that are in the world of the gods; surely you would conquer heaven, full of fame.
The human worlds and the divine, and the great worlds of Prajapati, and the whole kingdom of the gods are conquered, if Brihaspati officiates for you, lord of men."
[Samvarta] "Do not come to us again like this to hand Brihaspati to Marutta. I will not burn you with my terrible gaze, angered as I am; know this, fire."

[Vaishampayana] Then the smoke-bannered one went to the gods, afraid of burning and trembling like a pipal leaf. Seeing him, the great-souled Shakra said to the oblation-bearer in Brihaspati's presence:
Jatavedas, what did that king who is about to sacrifice say, when you were sent to give Brihaspati to Marutta? Does he accept my word?
[Agni] "Marutta does not like your word; he sent back Brihaspati's request, saying again and again that Samvarta will officiate for him.
And he said: 'Even if I could gain the human and divine worlds and the great worlds of Prajapati by making a pact with him, still I would not wish it.'"
[Indra] "Go again to that king and convey my message, suited to his own interest; if, being urged again, he will not do my word, then I shall hurl the thunderbolt at him."
[Agni] "Let the king of the gandharvas go there as messenger; I fear to go there, Vasava. Samvarta, sharp in anger and a practiser of celibacy, said to me in fury:
'If you come again like this to give Brihaspati to Marutta, I shall burn you with my terrible gaze; know that I am enraged, Shakra.'"
[Indra] "You burn others, Jatavedas; there is no other than you who reduces to ashes. All the world fears your touch; you speak what is unbelievable, oblation-bearer."
[Agni] "You could wrap heaven and earth in your own power, Shakra. With one such as you here, how did Vritra first seize heaven?"
[Indra] "It is not Chandika, nor a moving female elephant, nor water, fire; I do not drink soma, nor loose the thunderbolt against the weak. What man would strike me to my harm?
I drove the Kalakeyas out of the earth, I dragged the danavas from the sky, and brought Prahlada to his end from heaven. What mortal would strike me to my harm?"
[Agni] "Where Chyavana, about to officiate for Sharyati, alone took soma with the Ashvins, you in anger forbade it earlier; remember Sharyati's sacrifice, Mahendra.
Taking the thunderbolt, Purandara, you struck Chyavana terribly; that brahmin, enraged by austerity, seized your arm together with the bolt.
Then in anger he again produced for you a terrible enemy of every form: an asura named Mada, of universal form, whom you, seeing, closed your eyes.
One jaw of that great danava rested on the earth and one touched heaven; his thousand teeth, a hundred yojanas long and very sharp, were terrible.
His four round, thick fangs, silver-pillar-coloured, were two hundred yojanas; biting with his teeth, he ran at you with a terrible spear raised, wishing to kill you.
You saw him then in terrible form, and all others saw him too, awful to see; fearful, you came with folded hands to the great sage for refuge, slayer of danavas.
Thus Brahmic power is greater than kshatriya power; there is nothing greater than the brahmin. I, knowing Brahmic radiance as it is, do not wish to go to Samvarta, Shakra."
[Indra] "Dhritarashtra, go as sent to Marutta and tell him together with Samvarta: 'Take Brihaspati as officiant, king, or I shall hurl the terrible thunderbolt at you.'"
[Vaishampayana] Then Dhritarashtra went and spoke to the king this word of Vasava: "Know me as the gandharva Dhritarashtra; I have come, king, wishing to speak to you.

Hear Indra's word from me, lion among kings, which the lord of the worlds and great soul said: 'Choose Brihaspati as officiant, or I shall hurl the terrible thunderbolt at you. If you will not do this word of mine,' that is what he said, of inconceivable deeds."
[Marutta] "You know this, and Purandara, the Vishvedevas, Vasus and Ashvins: for betraying a friend there is no atonement, so the saying has always been in the worlds.
Brihaspati is the officiant of Mahendra, best of the gods and foremost of those who bear the thunderbolt; Samvarta will officiate for me today, O king; I do not like your word or his."
[The gandharva] "A terrible roar of Vasava, thundering in the sky, is heard, lion among kings. Mahendra will surely loose the thunderbolt on you; think of your safety, O king; this is the time."
So addressed by Dhritarashtra, the king, hearing Vasava's roaring, informed Samvarta, the best of knowers of dharma, ever in austerity, of the matter.
[Marutta] "This rock floats near; the road is long, so it cannot be seen today. I seek shelter from you, best of brahmins; give me freedom from fear, chief of brahmins."
[Marutta] "Let Indra himself come here at once, brahmin, accept the oblation at the sacrifice; let the gods enjoy their own seats and accept the soma pressed."
[Samvarta] "Here comes Indra with his bay horses, O king, together with all the gods, a soma-drinker, summoned by my mantras to this sacrifice today; see him, his body relaxed by the mantras."
[Vaishampayana] Then the king of the gods, with the gods, yoking the chief steeds to his chariot, came to the king's sacrifice, thirsting for the soma of the immeasurable son of Avikshit.
As he came with the hosts of gods, Marutta, with his priest, went to meet him and paid Indra the foremost honour, as the scriptures say, pleased.
[Samvarta] "Welcome, Purahuta, learned one; this sacrifice shines still more when you are present, Indra, slayer of Bala and Vritra. Drink the soma pressed and offered by me."
[Marutta] "Look on me with kindness; salutations to you. The sacrifice has come, my life is fruitful. Lord of the gods, this one, younger than Brihaspati by birth, performs my sacrifice."
[Indra] "I know him as your teacher, rich in austerity, Brihaspati's younger brother, of sharp radiance; summoned by whom I have come, king. I am pleased with you today; my anger toward you is lost."
[Samvarta] "If you are pleased, king of the gods, then yourself direct the arrangements at the sacrifice; make all the paths yourself, lord of the gods, and let this whole world know it, god."
[Vaishampayana] So addressed by Angiras's son, Shakra himself commanded the gods: "Let assembly halls and chief dwellings be made by the thousand, richly set with varied floors,
with posts set up, make ascents quickly for gandharvas and apsarases, where apsarases may dance by thousands; let the sacrificial ground be made like heaven."
So told, the dwellers of heaven quickly did it, pleased, by Shakra's word, O king. Then Indra, honouring Marutta, spoke to the king, pleased:

Here I am, king, come to you, and also your other earlier kings and all the other gods, pleased; let them accept your oblation.
mahabharata:14:10.29	Let them sacrifice the red victim to Agni, the many-formed shining one to the Vishvedevas, and the pure, blue bull for sacrifice; let the best of the twice-born sacrifice the shaking-organed one, as I directed.
Then the sacrifice of that king prospered, where the gods themselves bore away the food, where Shakra was honoured by brahmins and the wise king of the gods became a member of the assembly.
Then the great soul Samvarta, standing at the altar, like a second blazing fire, called the hosts of gods aloud with oblations and offered into the fire with mantras, well pleased.
Then, the slayer of Bala having drunk the best soma, and the other soma-drinking dwellers of heaven too, all were given leave by the king and departed, gratified as they liked and pleased.
Then the king, delighted, had heaps of gold made at every step, scattering vast wealth to the twice-born, and shone like the lord of wealth or the slayer of foes.
Then, having stored the varied wealth and filled his treasury as he wished, and given leave by his teacher, he returned and ruled the whole earth to the sea.
Such a king came to be here, in whose sacrifice that gold was abundant. Taking that wealth, king, sacrifice and gratify the gods by the rules."
[Vaishampayana] Then the Pandava king, delighted, hearing the words of Satyavati's son, set his mind to sacrifice with that wealth, and then took counsel again with his ministers.
The king, of dejected mind, his kin and relatives slain, was like the sun in eclipse or fire with smoke.
Knowing Partha disheartened, the upholder of the Vrishni line began to speak, consoling the son of Dharma.
[Vasudeva] "All that is crooked leads to death; uprightness is the path of Brahman. This much is the scope of knowledge; what use is idle talk?
Your task is not done, nor have your enemies been conquered; how is it you do not understand the enemy that lives in the body, the self?
On this I shall relate to you, by dharma and as heard, how the battle between Indra and Vritra went.
Once, O king, Vritra pervaded the earth, it is said; seeing the earth pervaded, her domain of smell taken, the earth's domain became foul from the taking.
Then Shatakratu grew angry that the domain of smell was taken, and, enraged at Vritra, he hurled the terrible thunderbolt.
Struck by the thunderbolt of great power on earth, he suddenly entered the waters and took their domain."
When Vritra had become space and its domain of sound was taken, Shatakratu, greatly angered, hurled the thunderbolt there.
Struck by the bolt of immeasurable power, he suddenly entered Shakra and then seized his domain.
When Vritra had seized him, a great delusion came over him; Vasishtha woke him with the Rathantara, dear one.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, Shatakratu killed Vritra in his body with an unseen thunderbolt; so we have heard.
This secret of dharma was told by Shakra to the great sages and by the sages to me; learn it, lord of men.
Disease arises in the body, it is bodily, without doubt; mental disease arises in the mind, that is certain.
Cold, heat and wind are the bodily qualities, O king; if there is balance among those qualities, they call it the mark of health. Heat is overcome by cold and cold by heat.
Goodness, passion and darkness are held to be the qualities of the self; if there is balance among them, they call it the mark of health. When any of them rises, a remedy is prescribed.
Sorrow is overcome by joy, and joy by sorrow. Someone in sorrow wishes to remember happiness; someone in happiness wishes to remember sorrow.
You, neither in sorrow wishing to remember sorrow nor in joy great happiness, son of Kunti, for fate is stronger.
Or this is your nature, by which you are drawn, Partha: seeing Krishna in the assembly in one garment, menstruating, before the Pandavas' eyes, you do not wish to remember that.
Nor your exile from the city, banishment in deer-skins and living in the great forest; you do not wish to remember that.
Nor the torment from Jatasura, the fight with Chitrasena, and the torment from the Saindhava; you do not wish to remember that.
For one freed from outer things yet greedy for bodily ones, whatever his dharma and happiness are, let them be for his enemies.
Death is the two-syllable word and eternal Brahman the three-syllable: 'mama' (mine) is two-syllabled death, and 'na mama' (not mine) is eternal.
Brahman and death, O king, both abide in the self; unseen, they surely make beings fight.
If the being's indestructibility is fixed, O Bharata, then by breaking the body, non-harm is attained.
Even having obtained the whole earth with moving and unmoving things, what will one do with it who has no sense of 'mine'?
Or he who lives in a forest, Partha, living on wild produce, and has attachment to things, lives in the mouth of death.
See, O Bharata, the nature of enemies outer and inner; the being that does not see it is freed from the great fear.
They do not praise a man full of desire in the world, nor is there any action without desire. Giving, Vedic study, austerity and Vedic rites are done by desire.
To one who strives to kill me with the Vedas, with the means of Vedanta, I appear as calm self, as in the immovable.
To one who strives to kill me with steadfastness, true valour, I become feeling, and he does not recognise me.
To one who strives to kill me with austerity, of sharp vows, I appear again in his austerity.
To the wise one who strives to kill me, resorting to liberation, abiding in joy of liberation, I dance and laugh; I alone am unkillable by all beings, eternal.
Therefore, you too, great king, do dharma with sacrifices of many fees, and that desire of yours will be there.
Sacrifice with the horse sacrifice, with due rule and fees, and with other varied sacrifices rich in fees.
Do not be pained, seeing your slain kinsmen again and again; those slain on this battlefield cannot be seen again.
Having sacrificed with great, rich sacrifices with fees given, you will win supreme fame in the world and go to the highest goal."
Consoled by the blessed Vyasa, Vishtarashravas himself, and Krishna Dvaipayana, and Devasthana,
and Narada, and Bhima, and Nakula, the king, and Krishna and Sahadeva, and the wise Vijaya,
and other tigers among men and brahmins who saw the scriptures, he gave up the grief born of sorrow and mental torment.
Yudhishthira honoured the gods and brahmins; and having performed the funeral rites for his kinsmen, the righteous king again ruled the earth to the sea.
His mind calm, the Kaurava, having gained his own kingdom entire, said to Vyasa, Narada and the others:

I have been consoled earlier by you, aged sages, best of ascetics; there is not even a subtle fault left in me here.
mahabharata:14:14.8	A great store of wealth has been gained by which I shall sacrifice to the gods; with you in front we shall assemble the sacrifice.
mahabharata:14:14.9	Guarded by you, Grandsire, we shall go to the Himalaya; that land is said to be full of marvels, best of the twice-born.
No unfortunate man gets such teachers, friends who, in calamity, are honoured by the good.
So addressed by the king, all the great sages, having taken leave of the king and of Krishna and Phalguna, vanished there as all watched.
Then the king, son of Dharma, sat down there; and so not very long a time passed for them.
While they performed purification rites, after Bhishma's death, giving great gifts to brahmins as funeral offerings,
he gave the funeral offerings for the Kurus with Bhishma and Karna at the head, joined with Dhritarashtra, delight of the Kurus.
Then, having given much wealth to brahmins, the best of the Pandavas, putting Dhritarashtra before him, entered Gajasahvaya.
Consoling his father, the lord with wisdom for eyes, the righteous one ruled the earth with his brothers.
[Vaishampayana] When the realm had been won by the Pandavas and was at peace, O lord of the people, Vasudeva and Dhananjaya were glad.
Joyful, they sported like two lords of the gods in heaven, in marvellous forests and on the slopes of mountains,
on lovely hills, in pools and rivers, roaming delighted like the two Ashvins in Nandana.
The great souls Krishna and the Pandava delighted at Indraprastha, and entering that lovely hall they played, O Bharata.
There, O king, at times they told varied tales of battle and of hardships, and tales of yoga.
They then told the lineages of sages and gods, those great souls, ancient best of sages, pleased.
Keshava, who knew the conclusion, told Partha sweet and varied tales, with varied meaning and well-fixed words.
Shauri Janardana calmed Partha, who was scorched by grief for his sons and thousands of kinsmen, with tales.
Having consoled him by rule, the great ascetic, knower of procedure, the Satvata, relieved of his own burden, seemed to rest.
Then, at the end of the tales, Govinda said to Gudakesha, consoling with soft speech, these reasoned words:

This whole earth was conquered, Savyasachin, scourge of foes, by the king, Dharma's son, relying on the strength of your arms.
mahabharata:14:15.13	Yudhishthira, king of dharma, enjoys a rival-less earth by Bhimasena's power and the twins', best of men.
mahabharata:14:15.14	By the righteous king, knowing dharma, a kingdom free of thorns has been gained; and King Suyodhana was slain in battle by dharma.
mahabharata:14:15.15	The sons of Dhritarashtra, with unrighteous tastes, greedy, ever speaking unpleasantly, evil-souled, were struck down with their relatives.
mahabharata:14:15.16	The whole earth is at peace, Partha; the king, Dharma's son, enjoys it, guarded by you, upholder of the Kurus.
mahabharata:14:15.17	I delight with you, Pandava, even in forests; how much more where there are these people and Pritha, scourge of foes?
mahabharata:14:15.18	Where the king, Dharma's son, is, where mighty Bhima is, where Madri's two sons are, there is my highest delight.
mahabharata:14:15.19	So too in these heaven-like regions of the hall, lovely and holy, with you, blameless one, I delight.
mahabharata:14:15.20	A long time has passed for me, hero, not seeing my father, and Baladeva, Kaurava, and the other Vrishni bulls.
mahabharata:14:15.21	So I wish to go to the city of Dvaravati; may my going please you too, best of men.
mahabharata:14:15.22	King Yudhishthira was told in many ways here and there what Bhishma said when we caused grief.
mahabharata:14:15.23	Yudhishthira was instructed by us, though he is himself an instructor; that great soul rightly took those words.
mahabharata:14:15.24	For in Dharma's son, knower of dharma, grateful and truthful, truth, dharma and the highest understanding and constant steadiness are ever fixed.
mahabharata:14:15.25	So go to that great soul, if it pleases you, Arjuna, and tell the king the words about our going.
mahabharata:14:15.26	I would not do him a displeasing thing even if life were at stake; how then should I go, mighty-armed one, to the city of Dvaravati?
mahabharata:14:15.27	All this I tell you, Partha, wishing your pleasure and good; I speak truth, Kaurava, not falsehood in any way.
mahabharata:14:15.28	My purpose in staying here is accomplished, Arjuna: King Dhritarashtra's son is slain with his army and followers.
mahabharata:14:15.29	The earth, dear one, is under the wise Dharma's son, standing sea-girt with her mountains, forests and groves, heaped with many jewels, Pandava, for the Kuru king.
mahabharata:14:15.30	May the king, knower of dharma, protect the whole earth by dharma, served by many perfected great souls and always praised by bards, best of the Bharatas.
mahabharata:14:15.31	So go with me today to the king, increaser of the Kurus, and ask leave to go to Dvaraka, tiger of the Kurus.
mahabharata:14:15.32	This body and the wealth that is in my house have been entrusted, Partha, always to Yudhishthira; Yudhishthira, the wise lord of the Kurus, is dear and honoured by me.
mahabharata:14:15.33	I have no purpose in staying, mighty-armed one, except for you; the earth stands under your rule, Partha, under that of the elder Yudhishthira of good conduct.
Thus spoke the great soul Janardana to the immeasurably valiant Arjuna; saying "So be it" as with effort, Arjuna honoured Janardana.
[Vaishampayana] Partha, with Krishna, having gained his own kingdom entire, sported joyfully in that lovely hall.
Then the two, by chance, glad and surrounded by their people, went to a part of the hall like a part of heaven, O king.
Then Pandava Arjuna, glad, with Krishna, looking at that lovely hall, said these words:

You know, mighty-armed son of Devaki's mother, the greatness you showed when the battle was at hand, and your divine form.
mahabharata:14:16.6	But what you said then, Keshava, out of love, all that, tiger among men, was lost to me, whose mind was lost.
mahabharata:14:16.7	I have curiosity about those matters again, lord, and you will go to Dvaraka before long, Madhava.
Thus addressed, Krishna, great in splendour and best of speakers, embraced Phalguna and replied.

I made you hear a secret and made known the eternal dharma in its own form, Partha, and all the eternal worlds.
mahabharata:14:16.19	[A brahmin said] Learned in many comings and goings, skilled in the meaning of the world's truth, knower of happiness and sorrow,
knowing the truth of birth and death, expert in merit and sin, seeing the course of embodied beings by their deeds, high and low,
moving as if liberated, perfected, at peace, with senses controlled, blazing with Brahmic glory, going about everywhere,
and knowing the way of vanishing: having heard truly of him, Kashyapa, and also of him going with the vanished perfected ones bearing discs,
conversing in private, sitting with them, and going by chance, unattached like the wind,
that wise best of brahmins, seeking dharma, an ascetic, well-concentrated, approached him and, as is proper, took his feet with supreme devotion.
Amazed at seeing that marvellous best of brahmins, Kashyapa pleased his teacher and physician with great service.
Pleased in soul, endowed with learning and conduct, the scourge of foes pleased him by his state of mind, with a pupil's conduct.
Pleased with that pupil, the teacher, gracious, said to him, looking to supreme perfection: 'Hear that from me, Janardana.
By various deeds and by pure merit alone, dear one, mortals go to a goal here and to a stay in the world of the gods.
Nowhere is there complete happiness, nowhere eternal standing; there is fall from a great station, and sorrow gained again and again.
I have met bad destinations, painful ones, by following sin, seized by desire and anger, by thirst and by delusion.
Again and again death, and again and again birth; various foods eaten, many kinds of breasts drunk.
Various mothers seen and fathers of different kinds, varied pleasures and sorrows, blameless one, by me.
Many separations from the dear and dwelling with the unloved, and loss of wealth gained with pain after getting it.
Insults, very painful ones, from others and from my own people, bodily and mental pains, terribly cruel.
I met fierce humiliations and cruel killings and bonds, falls into hell and tortures in Yama's realm.
Old age and diseases always, and many sufferings, pairs of opposites keenly experienced by me in this world.
Then, once, from disgust at wrongs and deceit, I gave up the world's business, deeply afflicted by sorrow; then this perfection was gained by me through the grace of the Self.
I shall not come back here again; I look at the worlds; until perfection, until the creation of beings, my course is good.
Best of brahmins, this supreme perfection has been gained. From here I shall go beyond, to the untroubled station of Brahma; let there be no doubt in you.
I shall not come here again in the mortal world, scourge of foes. I am pleased with you, greatly wise one; say, what shall I do for you?
The time has come for what you wish and for which you have come; I know it. I shall go before long; that is why I urged you.
I am greatly pleased with your conduct, discerning one; ask, as far as I can tell you what you wish.
I esteem your understanding and honour it greatly, by which you were awakened by me; you are wise, Kashyapa.'"
[Kashyapa] "How does the body fall, and how is it taken up? How, wandering, is one freed from the painful cycle of rebirth?
How, having yoked the self, does he leave the body, and how, freed from the body, does he enter another?
How does this man enjoy his good and bad deeds done by himself, and where does the deed abide for one without a body?"
[Brahmin] "Thus urged, the perfected one answered those questions in order, Vrishni; hear my words as they are.
[Perfected one] When in taking another body the deeds that bring life and fame have all been exhausted,
his soul seized with exhaustion of life, he follows contrary things, and his intellect is turned about when destruction is at hand.
Not knowing his own goodness, strength and time, the unrestrained one indulges excessively in things opposed to them.
When he indulges in everything very painful, or eats excessively, or never eats at all,
In entering the womb and in the crossing of vital parts, a man again gets such pain.
His joints broken, he gets wetness from the water, as he comes to rest in the five elements; by the cold the wind in the body, provoked, is driven fiercely.
That wind, abiding in the five elements as prana and apana, goes upward and, after pain, leaves the embodied one.
He leaves the body and is seen breathless, without heat, breathless, without lustre, without consciousness.
Abandoned by Brahman, the man is called dead. By the channels through which the embodied one knows the objects of the senses, by them he does not know the breath born of food.
That which acts there in the body is the eternal soul. Wherever each of them is joined at a meeting-point, know that vital part, for so it is seen in the scripture.
When those vital parts are pierced, it rises, enters the heart of the creature, and swiftly stops the goodness; then the creature, conscious, knows nothing.
His knowledge covered by darkness, his vital parts blocked, that soul, without a seat, is driven by the wind.
Then, breathing out that terrible great breath, going out it quickly shakes the unconscious body.
That soul, departed from the body, surrounded by its own deeds, marked by its good merits or by sins, is born again.
Brahmins endowed with knowledge and rightly firm in what they have learned know by marks which is the one of merit and which the other.
As the sighted see a glow-worm vanishing here and there in darkness, so those with the eye of knowledge see him.
Such perfected ones see the soul with divine eye, falling, being born, and entering the womb.
His places are seen here in the scripture as threefold: this earth is the land of action, where creatures stand.
Having done good or evil there, all embodied beings gain; here itself they obtain high and low enjoyments by their own deeds.
Here the doer of evil deeds goes to hell by his deeds; the sinful man is cooked sorely in hell, head downward. Therefore liberation is very hard to obtain, and the self must be guarded greatly.
Learn truly from me, as they are told here, the stations where creatures stand after going upward; hearing them, you would know the final understanding by certainty about action.
All the forms of the stars, and this orb of the moon, and the orb of the sun that shines in the world by its own light: know these as the places of men of meritorious deeds.
When their deeds are exhausted, all of them fall again and again; even there, in heaven, there is difference of low, high and middle.
All of them, Vidura and the rest, and the Pandavas, having eaten, attended that best of the Kurus, the king.
Know that I am Arjuna, and that Arjuna is I; whatever he says, understand that it must be done, Madhava.
The sixteen thousand women, Vasudeva's wives, plunged into the Sarasvati in time, O Janamejaya, and having become apsarases they went to Vasudeva.
